Now we must consider how these same realities appear one after another in the earthly world. To borrow the language of Qazi Sa'id Qummi, we are moving from the order of “subtle time” to that of “opaque time.”

We saw earlier, in broad terms, that the Shiite understanding of the Imams tries to answer a particular question: what does it mean, and what follows from it, to say that there will be no more prophets? We can understand the Shiite answer only if we first explore what prophecy itself means.

What makes someone a prophet? What kind of spiritual life and knowledge does a prophet possess? There are several possible answers, corresponding to different kinds of prophets. And those differences will reveal something important: prophecy is a wider calling than the particular mission of bringing a new religious law. A prophet—a nabi—is not necessarily, in the strict sense, a messenger sent with such a mission (a nabi mursal, or, in the fullest sense, a rasul).

Shiite teaching places walayat at the source of the prophetic calling, known as nubuwwat. The Persian word for walayat is dusti, friendship. We have already encountered the term. It refers especially to the divine love and friendship granted to the Twelve Imams from before the beginning of time. This gift makes them the “Friends of God,” or the “Beloved of God” (awliya Allah).

But walayat is not only the source of the prophetic mission. It also describes the spiritual state underlying prophecy in its broader sense, beyond the special mission of prophets who bring a new law.

A prophet who brings a law has an additional gift: he is sent by God to reveal a Book and a new sacred law (sharia). That law-giving mission belongs to a particular period of history. Walayat, by contrast, is eternal. It is what underlies the spiritual state of prophets as such.

Yet we must not confuse the terms. Once the law-giving prophet who is the “Seal of the Prophets” has appeared, there can be no further prophecy, even of the kind that introduces no new law, because there can be no new sharia. Before Islam, the simple word prophecy (nubuwwat) could cover prophets who did not bring a law; no separate term such as walayat was needed.

After the final Prophet, only walayat remains an appropriate name for this continuing spiritual gift. The gift itself, however, was present from the very beginning of the “cycle of prophecy.” With that cycle now closed, walayat emerges as the spiritual inheritance that prophecy has left to humanity.

Two questions follow. What exactly have the prophets left behind? And who inherits it? The Imams' own teachings answer both. The idea that prophecy has an eternal reality gives rise to the idea of someone on earth who inherits it spiritually: the Imam. Outside the wider picture established in the previous chapter, this answer may sound strange, even misplaced, to ordinary opinion, within Islam and beyond it. That is because it approaches the question from a different standpoint altogether.

Nevertheless, the answer was given from Islam's earliest days by people who traced their earthly descent from the Prophet through Fatima. Their family relationship was understood to reflect an eternal relationship within the complete company of heavenly beings, the pleroma. Fatima was called the “meeting place of the two lights” (majma' al-nurayn): the light of prophecy and the light of walayat. Whether people accepted or rejected the Imams' teaching has therefore shaped—and continues to shape—the spiritual destiny of Islam as a prophetic religion.

In the Shiite view, humanity's religious story did not end when prophecy came to an end. The very structure of our age or world-cycle, our Aeon, passes through the cycle of prophecy and then the cycle of walayat. It follows that further events still await us—not simply events of ordinary history, but events of sacred history.

To understand the Imam as the Prophet's spiritual heir, then, we need to look more closely at prophecy itself. Our first source is the body of traditions—the hadith and akhbar—handed down from the Imams. Many of them appear in the great collection assembled by Muhammad ibn Ya'qub Kulayni, a courageous Iranian Shiite theologian of the fourth Islamic century (tenth century CE), who died in 329 AH (940 CE). Kulayni lived long enough to know the last representatives (na'ib) of the Hidden Imam.
Indeed, his death came at roughly the time when the Imam's “Greater Occultation,” his longer period of hiddenness, began.
Kulayni's work is the oldest surviving comprehensive collection covering the major subjects of Shiite religious thought.

But it did not appear out of nowhere. Long before him, close disciples of the successive Imams had assembled smaller collections directly from what they heard. Some survive. Sadly, many are known to us only by their titles, preserved in other writings. Their manuscripts vanished during the upheavals faced by Shiite communities, which had to live more or less in hiding until the end of Abbasid rule in 1258. It is not our purpose here to recount those hardships, or the political unrest for which Shiite ideas could serve as a pretext.

The Imams' teachings, spread across thousands of pages, are religious teachings: they concern interpretation of scripture, moral life, worship, theology, and divine wisdom. They are never presented as a “political programme.” Shiite religious thought was preserved and developed not by politicians or agitators, but by the small circles of “faithful people whose hearts had been tested” who gathered around each Imam, even in the hardest circumstances.

As we stressed in the previous chapter, Shiite philosophical and religious thought—and what Shiites understand as its “history”—cannot be understood, still less lived, merely by standing outside it and explaining it in terms of external circumstances. The Imams saw this history as a spiritual history unfolding in the souls of their followers. It is made up of those followers' testimony, and the Imams themselves are the source from which their followers learn. That is why this “history” does not simply develop or evolve in the ordinary sense of those words.

Nor can we separate the Imams' teaching from the commentaries of those who lived it, reflected on it, and drew out its meaning because they believed in it. Their writings bear witness to their faith; their faith, in turn, made it possible for them to recognize everything contained in the teaching.

Here we meet again a principle we have had to affirm throughout this book. The historical reality of faith is not just a neutral sequence of external events that we can divide into equal stretches of chronological time. It is also the reality of faith itself, as each believer encounters what faith is directed towards, in the depth of the heart.

That is why our best guides to the holy Imams are the teachers who have commented on their words. They received those words as coming from the Imams and, because of their content, could understand them only in that way. The faith, thought, and writings of these teachers are themselves where the religious reality of Shiism—the reality of devotion to the Imams—comes alive in history.

Of course, this is not the kind of historical reality that ordinary historical criticism tries to establish when its main concern is to show that a particular Imam could not have spoken a particular saying. Such criticism may begin by destroying the object in which it does not believe. But once it has declared that object nonexistent, nothing remains for it to discuss.

We cannot regard a method that begins by destroying its own subject as a remarkable victory. I hope this book has shown why our study of religious experience tries instead to reach the religious reality as religious reality: to preserve the object of faith as it actually appears to the faith that encounters it. And no amount of historical criticism can alter this fact: for Shiite believers over thirteen centuries, a particular hadith has truly been spoken by a particular Imam, because its very content is understood as the Imam's own utterance.

So it should not be surprising that we have preferred, and will continue to prefer, the company of teachers who lived within the historical reality of Shiite faith. We have already met Haydar Amuli, Mulla Sadra Shirazi, Qazi Sa'id Qummi, and many others who sustained Shiite spiritual life. Mulla Sadra left us an immense commentary on the traditions collected by Kulayni.

When we are dealing with the realities of faith, the number of centuries separating two thinkers is not decisive. What matters is their closeness in intention and understanding: a kind of being together across time. We have already seen how this closeness makes possible philosophical reflection that never cuts itself off from spiritual practice. It also helps us understand why traditional Islamic philosophy continued to flourish in Shiite circles down to our own day.

If, then, we study with these Shiite teachers the sections of the great tradition collections devoted to prophecy and the Imams, we find that the teaching about prophecy gives especially clear expression to a central Islamic conviction: human beings need a guide to lead them along the “straight path” (sirat mustaqim) of their return to God. This is the path on which they remain faithful to the timeless covenant made with God before entering earthly life, as we saw in Chapter II. As far as the historical evidence allows us to trace the idea of prophecy and the special spiritual gift of the prophets, we cannot go back beyond the teachings of the Shiite Imams.

The question first takes shape through them, and Islamic thinking about prophecy grows from their teaching. There is a striking agreement between their arguments for the necessity of prophets and those later offered by philosophers such as al-Farabi, Avicenna, and Suhrawardi. They approach this necessity from two directions: from the human side and from the divine side.

For the philosophers who followed Avicenna, the aql—the intellect, or nous—remains only a potential ability in most people. Only in a few does the full human possibility become a living reality. These thinkers do not imagine a state of innocence in which people, simply following their natural impulses, could have built a society on their own. What passes for “natural law” would be what we call the law of the jungle. Avicenna and Biruni therefore hold that a divinely sent messenger, a prophet, is needed to establish law and justice.

Yet these philosophical arguments repeat what we find in the teachings of the Shiite Imams—for example, in the words of the Sixth Imam, Ja'far Sadiq (d. 148 AH/765 CE), preserved by Kulayni. Left entirely to themselves, people cannot find their way. They must come together in communities; but to do so they need someone who stands above the rest and shows them what is necessary both for safety in this life and for the life that continues beyond it.

The philosophers say that the fourth level of intellect—intellect fully at work—is reached by only a few individuals. Similarly, the Imams speak of five levels of Spirit (ruh), the highest of which, the Holy Spirit (ruh al-quds), is granted especially to the prophets.

For Imam Ja'far, however, the reason for this human inability is explained more directly from God's side. God, being beyond everything created, is inaccessible and invisible. No one has ever seen God or ever will. On this point Shiism differs from certain other Islamic schools: the Karramiyya allowed that God could be seen in this world and the next, and so conceived the vision in terms of space and dimensions; the Ash'arites allowed for vision in the next world, but without a face-to-face encounter or any spatial dimensions. After a long explanation of why no one can see or “touch” God, the Imam concludes:

It follows that there must be people who can command and forbid in the name of the All-Wise, All-Knowing One, and speak on His behalf. These are the people we call prophets (anbiya). They are the chosen ones among His creatures: sages (hukama) who have been taught by Wisdom (hikmat) and sent on their mission by Wisdom itself. They share with other human beings the fact of being created and the possession of a physical body. Apart from this, however, they do not share the same ways of being and acting as other people, because the All-Wise, All-Knowing One supports them and inspires them through Wisdom.

Such guidance remains available in every age and every period through the signs and proofs brought by the messengers and prophets. In this way God's earth is never left without a witness who stands as His proof (hujjat)—someone with a Sign (alam, a symbol) that shows the truth of what he says and the constancy of his justice.
This statement by Imam Ja'far raises three groups of questions.

1. The prophets as mediators. First, the prophets have a special qualification given by God that enables them to act as mediators. Following a long tradition, Mulla Sadra explains that prophetic existence has two sides. One faces divine transcendence and holiness (taqaddus); the other faces material reality and the human condition (tajassum). That is why a prophet can be called “a human being of divine standing” or “a divine lord in human form” (insan rabbani am rabb insani).

Both expressions are striking. They show that, from the beginning, Islamic thinking about prophecy and the Imams faced a problem similar to the one that divided the Nestorians and Jacobites in Eastern Christian debates about Christ.

Yet in Islamic prophecy, the divine qualification belongs only to the eternal prophetic reality—the Muhammadan Reality (haqiqat muhammadiya)—and not to the Prophet's earthly humanity (bashariyat). The Qur'an confirms his humanity in the words: “I am a human being like you, but divine revelation has come to me” (18:111). His divine reality, on the other hand, is suggested by another verse: “It was not you who threw when you threw; it was God who threw” (8:17).

2. How can God be seen? Second, as we have just read, the argument that prophets are necessary rests partly on the claim that God cannot be seen. The Imams' conversations with their close followers return to three related ideas: seeing God is impossible; God can be described only by the attributes God gives Himself; and God can be known only through God.
Yet, in the end, a certain kind of vision does prove possible. What kind of vision can that be?

a) Someone once wrote to the Eleventh Imam, Hasan Askari (d. 260 AH/874 CE), referring to a famous saying attributed to the Prophet—the hadith of the vision: “I saw my God in the most beautiful of forms.” The writer asked: “How could anyone worship a God whom he does not see?” The Imam replied: “Truly, God—blessed and exalted be He—made visible to the heart of His Messenger that light of His sublime majesty which the Messenger loved.”

This answer takes us into the territory of mystical experience. It introduces inner vision: seeing with the heart. It is love that makes vision possible—and love is itself the one being guided. What love sees is the very object it loves. The depth of the vision depends on the depth of the love. Mulla Sadra makes the point clearly. Most people see only through their bodily senses; their intellect (aql) never rises beyond a latent possibility. The “holy intellect” (intellectus sanctus, aql qudsi), which is the spiritual heart, is free from the limits of physical time and space.
b) A visitor, a Kharijite, once asked the Fifth Imam, Muhammad Baqir (d. 115 AH/733 CE): “What do you worship? God Most High? Have you seen Him?” The Imam answered:

No. Eyes do not see Him with their bodily power of sight, but hearts see Him through the realities (haqa'iq) of faith. He cannot be known by comparison (qiyas), whether by logical reasoning or analogy, and He cannot be grasped by the senses. His Signs (ayat) reveal how He may be described, and His symbols (alamat) make Him known. There is no violence in His judgments. Such is God, the God of whom we say: there is no god but Huwa—He.

c) The Sixth Imam, Ja'far Sadiq, also relates an answer given by the First Imam, the Commander of the Faithful, to a learned man who asked: “Commander of the Faithful, do you see your Lord when you worship Him?” The Imam replied: “Take care! I would never worship a God whom I did not see.” The man asked in return: “Then how do you see Him?” “Take care,” said the Imam. “Eyes do not see Him through physical sight. Hearts see Him through the realities of faith.”

The Imams' answers preserve a paradox. On one side stands the refusal given to Moses: “You shall not see Me” (lan tarani, 7:139). On the other stands the prophetic testimony: “I saw my God in the most beautiful of forms.”

Indeed, as we shall see in Chapter VII, the Imams' teaching led their followers towards a doctrine that agrees with Ibn Arabi's: a manifestation of God can be seen only in a form suited to the spiritual capacity of the person who sees it (mutajalla lahu). That person sees only his or her own form in the mirror of God; the Guide takes the form of the person being guided.

Vision of the heart, knowledge of the heart (ma'rifat qalbiya): these ideas appear repeatedly in the Imams' teaching. They do not belong exclusively to Sufism and were not invented by al-Ghazali (d. 505 AH/1111 CE). It is important to remember this whenever we ask about the relationship between Shiism and Sufism, or between the teaching about the Imams and mystical experience.

Let us turn to a remarkable passage from Mulla Sadra to see how fruitful this theme became for Shiite philosophers. It will keep returning throughout our study of prophets and Imams. Sadra asks us to think carefully about what we mean each time we use the word vision.

Among the followers of the later Imams, people often repeated a remark attributed to Hisham ibn al-Hakam, a famous young follower of the Sixth Imam. His argument bears a striking resemblance to certain ideas in Stoic physics: God, he said, must somehow be a body (jism). Otherwise God would be an act (fi'l, a verb)—something unreal that would only acquire concrete existence through the subject performing the action. What looks like a contradiction does not trouble Mulla Sadra greatly.

Unlike many earlier philosophers, he is concerned not primarily with the fixed essences of things but with their act of existing, and here his thinking too has affinities with Stoicism. One and the same essence can exist on different levels. That is true of what we call a “body,” from a body made of physical elements to a spiritual body. It is also true of the human being, whom Sadra understands in three parts. (A threefold understanding of the human being was abandoned in the West at the Council of Constantinople in 869.)
Here is that threefold picture. First comes the physical human being, with an organic body and the senses through which we perceive the physical world.

Second comes the psychic human being, whose “psychic body” has no parts that can be located within the dimensions of this world, because it does not belong to this world. Its way of perceiving depends on imagination and imaginative awareness, whose theory Mulla Sadra developed in particular depth.
Third comes the spiritual human being, with a “spiritual body” that possesses spiritual senses (hawass ruhaniya aqliya): spiritual sight, spiritual hearing, and so on.

That is why certain Qur'anic verses and hadiths must be understood at a spiritual level if we are to grasp them at the level where they actually speak—in what is, for that level, their true literal meaning. If the essence we call “body” can exist in different ways, on levels that differ in dignity and density, we can even imagine, at the furthest limit, something like a “divine body” (jism ilahi).
But we must immediately remember the Qur'anic words: “Nothing is like Him” (42:9).

The home of these spiritual senses is the heart. It is the heart that makes prophetic knowledge possible. For prophetic revelation and mystical experience belong to the same kind of spiritual reality, as Mulla Sadra explains:

The source of all mystical unveilings (mukashafat) is the human heart, through its very nature and its understanding of light, using the spiritual senses. For the heart has eyes, ears, and all the other senses. Many passages in the classical hadith collections confirm this. These spiritual senses are the source (asl) from which our bodily senses arise.

When the veil between the spiritual senses and outward reality is lifted, the source—the spiritual sense—and what comes from it—the bodily sense—are joined. What bodily senses perceive is then contemplated through the spiritual senses themselves. The Spirit (ruh) contemplates all this through its own power, because at its level all realities (haqa'iq) form a unity, just as they do for the Active Intelligence.
The heart therefore brings together every form and every level of the teaching about prophets and Imams.

3. Why the Imam must always be present. Third, this same idea of the heart leads us from the necessity of prophets to the necessity of the Imam. This is the last group of questions raised by the Sixth Imam's statement quoted earlier, where he insists that the earth can never be without someone who stands as God's witness or proof (hujjat). The idea is essential to Shiite teaching about the Imams.

From it comes the image of the “pole of the world,” even the “pole of poles,” without whom earthly existence could not continue for another instant. The image is familiar even in non-Shiite Sufism. We have already learned that the Imam, the pole, may be visible and known, or may be hidden, unknown to people, and beyond the reach of their bodily senses. According to the tradition, the latter is our own situation: the age of occultation (ghaybat), the age of the Hidden Imam.

How was this idea established in the first place? We have already seen its foundation. The prophet's task was to reveal the outward wording of the sacred law (sharia). The task of another was to teach its inner spiritual meaning (ta'wil). That other person is the Imam, the “Guardian of the Book” (qayyim al-Qur'an), who keeps its meaning alive.

The Sixth Imam's hadith brings us to this conclusion: God must send prophets, because the great human task is to find the way to live faithfully by the timeless covenant made with God. “Am I not your Lord?” (a-lastu bi-rabbikum?), God asks in the Qur'an (7:171). People cannot find that way without a guide, and that guide is the prophet.
But what happens when the prophet is no longer there? More urgently still, what happens when the prophet who has departed was the final Prophet?

A follower named Mansur ibn Hazim once told Imam Ja'far about his conversations with Muslims who were not Shiites. He would ask them the crucial question: “Now that God's Messenger is no longer here, who will stand before humanity as the witness, the one who can give the decisive answer (hujjat)?” Usually they replied: “The Qur'an.”

But Mansur had studied the Qur'an himself. He knew how fiercely people disagreed about what its words meant. So he had concluded that the Qur'an alone could not serve as the decisive witness without a guardian (qayyim), an interpreter (mufassir), who knew its full inner truth (haqiqat). This guardian is the Imam: the Guide.

Mulla Sadra, for his part, argues that this central Shiite teaching follows directly from the fact that God is beyond everything else. Philosophy teaches, he says, that whatever has no cause—the uncaused ground, the Abgrund—cannot have its essence defined or be proved by appealing to something else. All other proofs begin from it. We know things that have causes through those causes.

But how can we know the One who causes all causes (musabbib al-asbab) and makes every cause knowable? That is the meaning of the First Imam's saying: “I have never known anything without knowing God before it.” A mystic echoes the same thought: “I know my God only through my God.”
To “know one's God” is to know God's attributes.

But how could we reach such knowledge without either a divine message brought by an angel (wahy) or divine inspiration (ilham)? Those who know about the “origin” and the “return” (mabda' and ma'ad) have received one of these two gifts. The prophets receive the message through an angel. The Imams and the Friends of God receive inspiration, whether in dreams or while awake. This kind of inspired knowledge is what we call sacred knowledge or hierognosis. Everyone who has received neither kind must turn to God's messengers, the prophets.
Yet the question immediately returns: whom are we to seek when there is no longer a prophet?

We now have the basis of the argument. A living witness (hujjat) must always be present, because the Qur'an by itself cannot perform that role. The Qur'an has an outward meaning and an inward meaning (batin)—indeed, tradition speaks of as many as seven inner depths. It is a book of symbols, whose meanings are not immediately visible. Mulla Sadra declares:

The Qur'an is not a book that can be understood through the ordinary knowledge of philosophers. Most educated people already find it difficult to understand the philosophers' books, whether those of the ancients, such as Plato and Aristotle, or those of more recent writers, such as al-Farabi and Avicenna. How, then, could they understand the Qur'an—the divine speech that comes from God and descended into the heart of His Prophet?

Who could guide people through its many hidden meanings, unless that person possessed an inward sight (basirat) illuminated by God, and a spiritual hearing (sama' aqli) able to hear from God and His angels—even without seeing an angel's form or hearing the sound of its speech, as the Prophet himself saw and heard through these two spiritual senses?

As we shall see, the difference between prophets on the one hand and Imams and Friends of God on the other does not lie in whether they possess this sacred knowledge. It lies in the way they receive it and the degree to which they possess it.

Anyone who possesses this double power of spiritual sight and hearing—even if it does not equal that of a prophet-messenger—is therefore capable, after the Prophet, of guarding the Book in the fullness of its meaning. That person is the Imam. We have already noted that this answer to the problem of succession does not appeal to a Church, an official body of religious teachers, or any collective authority. It appeals to a person of God, inspired by God. In this sense, the very need to interpret revelation becomes a scriptural argument for the necessity of the Imams.

On the deepest level of their being, as we have already learned, the Imams inherit a spiritual reality from prophecy, and they have been entrusted with that inheritance from before the beginning of time. Here the argument for Ali ibn Abi Talib's position as Imam rests on something more specific: among all the Prophet's companions, he alone knew the complete meaning of the revelations. Whenever a verse of the Qur'an was revealed, the Prophet dictated it to Ali, made him repeat it, and taught him both its outward explanation (tafsir) and its inner spiritual meaning (ta'wil). Ali himself relates:

And the Prophet prayed to God to enlarge my understanding and strengthen my memory. From the time he made that prayer for me, I have not forgotten a single verse of the Book or a single piece of knowledge that he dictated to me.
Texts like these help us understand the very heart of Shiism. One can only wish they were more widely known—and, above all, better understood—in the West.

The point becomes even clearer when we discover that the Imam, as “Guardian of the Qur'an,” is identified with the heart. Here we meet again the young Hisham ibn al-Hakam, who stood out among the companions of the Sixth Imam both for his youth and for the fierce devotion he felt towards the Imam. On one occasion, the boy decided on his own to challenge a leading Mu'tazilite teacher, Abu Marwan Amr ibn Ubayd, who held public discussions in Basra. The Mu'tazilites represented a tradition of reasoned theological debate within Islam.

The Imam later asked Hisham to tell him about this bold expedition into argument. Hisham had jumped onto his camel and ridden from Kufa to Basra, where he found the teacher giving his Friday lesson in the mosque, surrounded by disciples. It was a solemn gathering.

But Hisham asked to speak and began posing questions that the teacher at first found absurd. “Do you have eyes?” he asked. “What do you do with them?” He went on in the same way through each of the five senses.

The teacher played along. That allowed Hisham to reach his final question. In the teaching about the body's subtle inner faculties, the heart—as the seat of awareness—is what finally decides whether information from the senses is trustworthy or doubtful. In that sense, the heart is the Imam, the guide, of our bodily perceptions. The Mu'tazilite teacher had to agree that he possessed such a heart. Hisham then replied:

Abu Marwan! So God has not abandoned the organs of your senses without giving them an Imam—one who confirms what is true and enables them to settle their doubts. Would God, then, have left all human beings to their confusion, doubts, and bewilderment, when He has given you an Imam to whom your own senses can bring their doubts and confusion?

It is especially important that the need for an Imam is established here by comparing the wider world with the smaller world of the human being. At the very moment when we discover why the human community needs an Imam, a path opens towards finding the Imam within the spiritual life of each person. The teaching about the Imams meets the most personal kind of spiritual fulfilment.

What is said about the Imam's role in the community continually sheds light on what takes place in each person's inner life, and the reverse is also true. A believer's chosen bond with one of the Imams can be experienced as the presence of an inner guide.

In Ismaili thought, for example, this insight developed into the symbolism of Mount Sinai and the olive tree. Mount Sinai stands for the mystic. At its summit—or in its heart—grows the olive tree, which represents the Imam: the “soul of the soul” (jan-e jan), the mystic's personal inner guide.

We can go further. In the light of what we have learned about the spiritual senses, realities belonging to the inner world must be understood literally at their own level. That is how Mulla Sadra reads Hisham's story. As we saw in Chapter V, at each spiritual station (maqam) the spiritual truth is the literal truth proper to that station. Sadra writes:

The heart is a subtle body of light (latifa nuraniya). It must be distinguished from the cone-shaped organ of flesh (qalb sanawbari). The thinking soul (nafs natiqa) is the leader and Imam of all its powers. The heart, as the soul's permanent dwelling and the throne on which it sits, is the leader and Imam of the organs through which those powers work.

The same relationship holds on the larger scale. It is essential for life that the sign of the Imam should stand in every age. That is why the invisible presence of the “Hidden Imam” is necessary, even during a period of occultation (ghaybat) such as our own. According to Mulla Sadra, this conclusion about divine wisdom holds regardless of the differences between sacred laws (sharia) and religions. For, as Imam Ja'far tells the young Hisham in approval, it is written in the divine Books (kutub ilahiya) and the heavenly Psalms (zubur samawiya): “in the books of Abraham and Moses” (87:19).

As Mulla Sadra reminds us, this is where the question that divided Islam from within comes into focus. What makes someone an Imam? Why must an Imam be present in every age, whether openly known or hidden from most people? The Shiite answer becomes clearer once we return to a distinction we made earlier: the divine communication (wahy) received by prophets sent with a mission, and the inspiration (ilham) granted to the Imams and God's friends.
By distinguishing prophets according to how they receive knowledge, the Shiite understanding of prophetic knowledge also tells us where the Imam belongs in the wider story of prophecy.

Put another way, the future of the community as a spiritual community depends on what it accepts or rejects of this philosophy of prophecy. This is why I have placed that philosophy at the very foundation of philosophical thought in Islam—although my reasons have not always been understood. For the thinkers who sustained Islam's spiritual consciousness, it was through reflection on prophecy that they came to understand Islam's calling in the world.
2. The Different Kinds of Prophets and Walayat
The Arabic word for prophet, nabi, comes from forms of a root meaning “to bring someone news.” A nabi is someone who brings news from God (mukhbir 'an Allah).

But what, in its deepest sense, makes someone a prophet? Mulla Sadra says that we cannot answer until we have explained how knowledge is placed—or, in his own striking image, “cast”—by God into the human heart (ilqa al-'ulum).

In seeking an answer, Shiite philosophers developed a theory of knowledge from the teachings about prophecy passed down by their Imams. This is a distinctive feature of the philosophy that grew out of Shiism, or the inner, spiritual understanding of Islam. It sees the Holy Spirit, Gabriel—the angel who brings revelation—as fundamentally the same being as the angel through whom knowledge becomes possible, what philosophers call the Active Intellect.

We must not mistake this for an attempt to reduce revelation to ordinary reason. The Arabic word 'aql has a wider meaning than the English word reason. It can describe forms of understanding ranging from the philosopher's fully awakened intellect to the sacred understanding of a prophet. And Mulla Sadra's central claim is not about abstract reasoning at all. It is about the heart, and the way truth can become present within it.

The human heart (qalb al-insan)—always the central image here—is, by its very nature, capable of receiving the reality of anything that can be known. Such knowledge may come through religious teaching: sacred texts and the established religious sciences ('ulum shar'iya).

Or it may come directly from the giver of knowledge, the Holy Spirit understood as divine Intelligence ('Aql, Ruh). That is why the sciences called 'ulum 'aqliya cannot simply be equated with what we call rational knowledge. They can reach beyond philosophy in its usual sense. Broadly understood, they are the spiritual sciences.

Mulla Sadra divides these forms of spiritual knowledge into two groups: truths known from the outset, such as first principles, and truths that must be acquired. Acquired knowledge may come through teaching (ta'allum) and the indirect work of reasoning. This is the path of philosophers and scholars who build arguments.
